cues.text: By 1630, the small mountain village of Canosio, in northern Italy’s Val Maira region, had grown noticeably lax in its religious observance.
Calvinist teaching spread through the surrounding valleys, drawing some residents away from their Catholic upbringing’s practices.
The day after the feast of Corpus Christi that year, torrential rain sent the Maira River into violent flood.
Massive stones were dislodged from the surrounding mountainside, threatening to sweep away both the valley and the village itself in the rushing water.
A Priest Walks Toward the Flood
Rather than flee, the parish priest, Father Antonio Reinardi, placed the Blessed Sacrament in a monstrance.
He processed with a group of the faithful directly toward the rising floodwaters, reciting Psalm 51, the Miserere, as they approached the danger rather than retreating from it.
According to the tradition kept in Canosio ever since, Father Reinardi raised the monstrance and blessed the oncoming flood.
The waters that had threatened to destroy the village turned back or subsided at that moment, sparing the community the destruction that had seemed imminent only moments before.

The event reportedly produced a wave of renewed devotion among villagers whose faith had cooled in the years before, and Canosio has marked the anniversary every year since with a feast during the Octave of Corpus Christi.
The Canosio account differs from the theft- and doubt-centered traditions common elsewhere in this exhibition.
Instead, it centers on a pastor's direct, physical act of confronting danger with the Sacrament rather than in spite of it—a priest who met a flood by walking toward it.
